name: no-time
title: No time to type
kicker: Why this talk · the second ground has four legs
html:
No time to type

Family, a new dog, a phone in one hand and a leash in the other.

Half the fix: /remote-control

The session runs at home; I steer it by thumb from the sidewalk.

The other half: rigour without watching

Same behaviour every time, BDD followed strictly: Gherkin, red, code, green, commit.

Hooks, not hopes

A write out of order is refused. Every run is logged. The commit gate checks the order. I read the record, not the agent.

Controls that hold while nobody watches. That’s this talk. hooks.json

/remote-control

Please give me an update

Red run logged. Writing the fix.

How’s it going?

Green. Commit gate: TDD order checked.

🐕 pulling. back in 20

Illustrative, not a transcript. The two questions are the real ones, every evening. So is the dog.
say: The second ground is personal, and it has four legs. Family, and a new dog. Typing time is gone: one hand holds a leash, the other a phone. Half the fix was Claude Code's /remote-control: the session runs on my machine at home, and I steer it by thumb from the sidewalk. Most evenings that's two prompts: 'Please give me an update', and 'How's it going?' But that's only half. An agent I can't watch has to behave the same way every time, and it has to follow BDD rigorously: Gherkin first, a red run, the code, a green run, then a commit. Asking it nicely isn't enough; instructions are advisory. So hooks enforce it: a write out of order is refused, every run is logged, and the commit gate checks the order. I don't monitor the agent; I read the record when I get home. Hold on to that: controls that hold while nobody watches. It's exactly what this talk asks of agents calling APIs.
